<Rep. Maxine Waters, Rep. Nydia M. Velázquez, Rep. Stephen F. Lynch, Rep. Al Green, Rep. Emanuel Cleaver, Rep. Joyce Beatty, Rep. Juan Vargas, Rep. Rashida Tlaib, Rep. Sylvia R. Garcia, Rep. Nikema Williams, Rep. Cleo Fields>: Furthermore, this bill ignores the lessons from the failure of Silicon Valley Bank and other regional banks which failed a few short years after Congress and President Trump's regulators rolled back enhanced prudential standards on these banks. Instead, this bill lets even more of these regional banks escape critical safeguards that promote safety and soundness. Instead of rolling back progress to pursue deregulation that enables unnecessary risk-taking, speculation, and weakens our financial system, we should work together to strengthen community banks, credit unions, and consumer protections, as well as promote access to affordable financial products and services.
Committee Democrats offered several amendments to improve the bill that were rejected. This included an amendment from Ranking Member Waters that would provide funding and reforms to support community development financial institutions (CDFIs) and minority depository institutions (MDIs). This was based on her bill, H.R. 9767 (118th Cong.), the ``Promoting and Advancing Communities of Color Through Inclusive Lending Act.'' The Majority rejected another amendment by Ranking Member Waters to strip the bill of harmful provisions that would roll back various consumer protections. It would have also restored the CFPB of its original funding levels from the Federal Reserve, and required the CFPB to resume supervision of the largest banks that compete with community banks at the same frequency and with the same number of staff as in 2024.
The Majority rejected another amendment by Ranking Member Waters to modernize the deposit insurance framework and enhance tools to hold culpable executives of a failing bank accountable. The latter amendment was based on her legislation, H.R. 4551, the ``Employee Paycheck and Small Business Protection Act,'' and H.R. 7886, the ``Failed Bank Executives Accountability and Consequences Act.'' Finally, the majority rejected an amendment from Rep. Sean Casten to require the Federal Reserve to report on any activities they have carried out as Treasury's fiscal agent relating to Venezuela's oil proceeds.
There were a number of organizations that either opposed H.R. 6955 or bills included in the package, including: Americans for Financial Reform (AFR), Center for Responsible Lending (CRL), Consumer Action, Consumer Federation of America, Consumer Reports, Institute for Agriculture and Trade Policy, Interfaith Center on Corporate Responsibility, National Association of Consumer Advocates, National Community Reinvestment Coalition (NCRC), National Consumer Law Center, on behalf of its low-income clients (NCLC), National Consumers League, New Economy Project, Private Equity Stakeholder Project, Public Citizen, Public Justice Center, Rise Economy, The People's Justice Council, Transparency Task Force, and 20/ 20 Vision.
For these reasons, we oppose H.R. 6955.
APPENDIX--ADDITIONAL DETAILS AND ANALYSIS OF OTHER SECTIONS OF THE BILL
Below is a section-by-section description and analysis of the other sections in H.R. 6955. Title I--New Bank Formation and Local Community Access
• Sec. 101: H.R. 478--the ``Promoting New Bank
Formation Act'' (Barr), (4/2/25 markup, 28-21). This
section, which Republicans passed through Committee
last Congress by a party-line vote, requires new banks
and their holding companies to have lower capital
requirements than they otherwise should have for their
first three years, with additional capital reductions
for rural de novo community banks by allowing them to
be subject to below 8% Community Bank Leverage Ratio
(CBLR) in their first two years before reaching 8% in
their third year. New banks are much more vulnerable to
failure than other banks, which is why appropriate
capital is key to ensure they can stay in business and
grow. There were technical changes in the amendment in
the nature of a substitute (ANS), for example, adding a
U.S. Code citation, but substantively this is the same
as the standalone version of H.R. 478 instead of the
more targeted, pilot program version that Democrats
agreed to include in the Housing for the 21st Century
package.
• Sec. 102: H.R. 6551--the ``New Bank
Application Numbers Knowledge (New Bank) Act''
(Loudermilk), (12/17/25 markup, 53-0). The section
would require annual reports relating to applications
for new Federal depository institution charters, bank
holding companies, credit unions, Federal deposit
insurance, and State depository institution charters.
It would require the reporting of timelines and common
reasons for denial of such applications.
• Sec. 103: H.R. 6536--the ``Rural
Depositories Revitalization Study Act'' (Norman), (12/
17/25 markup, 50-0). The section would require the Fed,
FDIC, OCC, and NCUA to study ways to improve the
growth, capital adequacy, and profitability of rural
depository institutions, as well as the creation of de
novo depository institutions in rural areas. The ANS
modifies this section to provide for two separate
studies--one by the 3 banking regulators, and a
separate one by NCUA. This previously was section 104
in the introduced version; the old section 103 was
moved down in the bill to become section 604.
• Sec. 104: H.R. 5913, the ``Community
Investment and Prosperity Act'' (Lawler)--increase
public welfare investment (PWI) cap for banks, included
in Housing for 21st Century. This section was added by
the ANS and would increase the public welfare
investment cap for the OCC and the Federal Reserve from
15% to 20% to enhance the capacity of banks to make
investments in affordable housing and would require the
OCC and Federal Reserve to study and publish routine
reports on how these investments are made and used to
support communities.
• Sec. 105: H.R. 3161 (118th), the ``CDFI Fund
Transparency Act'' (Rose), (5/16/24 markup, voice
vote). This section was added by the ANS and requires
the Treasury Secretary (or their designee) to testify
annually on the CDFI Fund. This section does not
include reporting requirements that were added by
Ranking Member Waters, Rep. Velazquez, and Rep. Beatty
when the bill was passed by voice vote through the
Committee in 2024. Those omitted Democratic provisions
were designed to gain more granular data and better
learn how Treasury and the CDFI Fund were taking steps
to support community financial institutions.
• Sec. 106: H.R. 7733 (117th), the ``CDFI Bond
Guarantee Program Improvement Act'' (Cleaver) (5/17/22
markup, voice vote), previously passed in 2022 by FSC
and House by voice vote. This section was added by the
ANS bill and would reauthorize and improves the CDFI
Bond Guarantee Program. Specifically, the section
lowers the CDFI Bond Guarantee Program minimum issuance
threshold from $100 million to $25 million to expand
access, and revises the amount to be held in a CDFI's
relending account. Instead of extending this program by
4 years as the Committee and the House previously
approved in the 117th Congress to provide certainty to
market participants, this section would only extend the
program until 2028. Title II--Tailoring Bank Regulation
• See description of Section 201 (H.R. 3380,
the ``Taking Account of Institutions with Low Operation
Risk (TAILOR) Act,'' Loudermilk) and Section 202 (H.R.
2835, the ``Small Bank Holding Company Relief Act,''
Donalds) above in the section on poison pills.
• Sec. 203: H.R. 5276--the ``Community Bank
Leverage Improvement and Flexibility for Transparency
(Community Bank LIFT) Act'' (Kim), (9/16/25 markup, 33-
19). This section would permit community banks to have
significantly less capital by lowering the statutory
range for the community bank leverage ratio (CBLR) from
8-10% to 6-9% (the standalone bill provided a range of
6-8%, the ANS modified this to 6-9%). Trump's
regulators in his first term previously set the CBLR at
9%, though more recently have proposed lowering this to
8%. However, most community banks (83%) have over 9%
CBLR, but are not utilizing the CBLR framework for
other reasons, raising serious questions that reducing
the CBLR ratio is necessary for more banks to utilize
the framework. The section also increases the threshold
from $10 billion to $15 billion.
• Sec. 204: H.R. 6553--the ``Tailoring and
Indexing Enhanced Regulations (TIER) Act'' (Barr), (12/
17/25 markup, 33-19). This section would significantly
increase the thresholds for enhanced prudential
standards (i.e. capital, liquidity, stress testing,
risk management, etc.) that apply to the largest banks.
Specifically, the bill increases the threshold when
mandatory enhanced standards apply from $250 billion to
$370 billion in assets, and the minimum threshold for
when regulators have the discretion to apply such
standards from $100 billion to $150 billion. As we
approach the three year anniversary when we had 3 of
the 4 largest bank failures in U.S. history and
regulators were forced to use systemic risk tools to
resolve Silicon Valley Bank ($212 billion) and
Signature Bank ($110 billion), this approach ignores
lessons from that crisis and will reduce safeguards
relating to these large institutions. Furthermore, the
section indexes these thresholds to rapidly grow based
on nominal GDP (e.g. between 2015 and 2025, nominal GDP
grew by 67%, compared to 25% growth based on real GDP),
an approach Trump's FDIC recently rejected when
adjusting much smaller regulatory thresholds when they
adopted an inflation-based approach to index such
thresholds.
• Sec. 205: H.R. 7056, the ``Community Bank
Regulatory Tailoring Act'' (Barr), (1/22/26 markup, 33-
21). This section was added by the ANS. The section,
which the Committee did not hold a hearing on,
increases 37 regulatory thresholds for financial
institutions regarding a wide range of topics,
including capital, consumer protections, fair lending,
anti-discrimination, community reinvestment, Volcker
Rule's prohibition on proprietary trading, executive
compensation, GAAP accounting, independent audits, and
more without any study or analysis to justify these
changes. These thresholds are in a number of Federal
banking and consumer protection laws, specifically, the
Bank Holding Company Act of 1956 (``BHCA''), Community
Reinvestment Act of 1977 (``CRA''), Depository
Institution Management Interlocks Act (``DIMIA''),
Dodd-Frank Wall Street Reform and Consumer Protection
Act (``Dodd-Frank''), Federal Credit Union Act, Federal
Deposit Insurance Act (``FDI Act''), Federal Home Loan
Bank Act of 1932 (``FHLB Act''), Federal Reserve Act,
Home Mortgage Disclosure Act of 1975 (``HMDA''), Home
Owners' Loan Act (``HOLA''), International Lending
Supervision Act of 1983, Real Estate Settlement
Procedures Act of 1974 (``RESPA''), Revised Statutes of
the United States (which includes the National Bank
Act), and Truth in Lending Act (``TILA''). Some of
these thresholds have not been adjusted in decades and
would include sizable increases with little
justification. Instead of focusing on small
institutions, several of the threshold increases would
benefit large banks with up to $175 billion in assets,
and all of the changes reduce safeguards with no
threshold changes that would benefit consumers.
Furthermore, these revised thresholds would all
continue to rapidly grow based on nominal GDP, an
approach that Trump's FDIC recently found to be
inappropriate and too aggressive when they updated some
similar thresholds using a more modest and typical
inflation-based indexing approach.
• Sec. 206: H.R. 975, the ``Credit Union Board
Modernization Act'' (Vargas). This section was added by
the ANS, and previously passed House several times with
broad bipartisan support, including in the Housing for
21st Century Act. This section would reduce board
meeting requirements for well-managed credit unions,
aligning Federal standards with similar credit union
board requirements for many states. Title III--Fair and Transparent Bank Supervision
